cse-2017-1-cs-15.approach: A birthday attack finds *some* pair of messages with the same hash; only someone who controls which message gets signed — the signer S — can exploit such a pair.

steps.title: What a birthday attack gives
steps.body: About $2^{k/2}$ work for a $k$-bit hash yields two messages $m, m'$ with $H(m)=H(m')$ — but the attacker cannot choose one of them to be a fixed, already-signed message.

steps.title: S can use it
steps.body: S prepares a colliding pair, signs $m$, and later claims (or substitutes) $m'$ — the signature verifies for both. Violation (I) is possible.

steps.title: Third party and R cannot
steps.body: They see a message $m$ already signed by S. To substitute, they need $m'$ with $H(m')=H(m)$ for that **given** $m$ — a second pre-image problem ($\approx 2^k$ work), not a birthday attack. So (II) and (III) are not birthday-attack violations.

optionAnalysis.reason: A third party faces a fixed signed message, so it needs a second pre-image, not a birthday collision.
Only the signer chooses which message of a colliding pair gets signed.
The third party cannot pre-arrange a collision with a message it did not author.
Neither R nor a third party can mount a birthday attack against a message they did not choose.

pitfalls: Treating any hash-substitution as a birthday attack — the birthday bound applies only when the attacker generates both colliding messages.
